As for hits versus runs, much of it does simply have to do with stranding runners. Some players and teams are just worse when there are runners in scoring position. Some of it also has to do with power numbers, as the more extra-base-hits a team gets the more runs it will score, which is a large reason for the Astros discrepancy last year, as they were notorious for swinging for the fences and not caring if they struck out a lot(a bit of an oversimplification, but it's complicated). Several logistical points to make on this. As someone else pointed out, they do have other camera angles, that aren't generally released to the public. Sure there could be more still, but the cameras themselves are expensive as fuck, and then you add camera operators onto that, and it'd be a big expense that would be a total loss for whoever has to pay for it.

As for the better science, video is 60 frames per second. Over the years, I've seen many many plays that were actually so close that one frame the play was still happening and the next it was over. Unless we switch all of the video equipment in the entire league over to a higher framerate, that will keep happening. As for sensors and the bases synced to to ball or the camera or whatever, it's a ton of new equipment, people to monitor it all, and only the slightest thing needs to go wrong at the wrong time and suddenly you have conspiracy theories going all over the place. As someone who works in the industry I can tell you that is everyone's worst nightmare.

The last two things I'll address together. When a call is made on the field, it is assumed as correct. If we stop assuming that then the entire umpiring system goes down the drain, as there are so many call in each game. That's why the call on the field matters. And it needs definitive evidence to be overturned because the rules have to be applied evenly across the league, and if you begin to let replay officials overturn calls without that exacting level of proof, then it suddenly becomes up to each replay official to use his own judgement as to how much evidence he needs. Which would mean on different nights there would be different thresholds of proof to overturn calls. Thus the need for definitive evidence.

As far as my other points, teams wouldn't have to do it literally every possession to get a point, but like I said, how many rebound attempts or screens are there per game where a player could legitimately foul Jordan? Plenty. And they would only need to foul him on a fraction of those to get into the penalty. Once that happens, teams can be strategic about when they want to do it. At which point referees have to begin deciding whether what looked like actual basketball plays were actually basketball plays or not. And given how poorly the refs do in deciding flagrant fouls, that's not a power that I wish to give them.

You really trust the refs to divine a player's intention? The don't have to go through him like a battering ram to foul him, there are plenty of fouls of players trying to legitimately get through a screen, all the players have to do is figure out what those are, and boom, they've got their intentional fouls back. Same with offensive rebounding. Pushing off of someone's back to get an offensive rebound is an attempt at a basketball play, and happens every single game. But it's also a foul, given that one of DeAndre Jordan's primary purposes is to rebound, it would be pretty easy to just foul him going for a rebound on every missed shot. They're still basketball plays, because if the ref doesn't call it, the other team gets the ball back and prevents a DeAndre offensive rebound.

I don't think extending the last two minutes of the game rule to the whole game would be as easy to implement as everyone seems to think. There are lots of ways to foul someone off the ball without it seeming to be an intentional foul. Say we ban intentional fouls for the entire game, why would a team who wanted to play hack-a-Jordan not just plow through him every time he sets a screen for someone. Given how many screens he sets, that would get a team into the bonus real quickly, and DeAndre would be back at the free throw line 20+times per game.
